# Verdict: REVISE ## Overall Assessment The component implements a well-structured registration form with correct semantic HTML, proper label associations, and a coherent error summary pattern. The core architecture (error summary + inline errors + `aria-describedby`) is sound. However, the **dual announcement pattern** — combining `role="alert"` on the summary with `aria-live="polite"` on every inline error wrapper — creates a redundant, confusing screen reader experience that deviates from the GOV.UK pattern the developer cites as their reference. This is the primary design flaw and is fixable with a small, targeted change. ## Pre-commitment Predictions Before reading the code, I predicted: | # | Prediction | Result | |---|-----------|--------| | 1 | Dual announcement: `role="alert"` + `aria-live` on inline errors will cause screen readers to announce errors twice | **CONFIRMED** — primary finding | | 2 | Error summary links (`href="#field-…"`) may not move focus in SPA context | **PARTIALLY** — works in browsers, but fragile in SPAs | | 3 | Error summary re-announces when content changes (user fixes one field) | **CONFIRMED** — consequence of `role="alert"` + content mutation | | 4 | Missing `autocomplete` attributes on email/password/name fields | **CONFIRMED** — minor gap | | 5 | No required-field indication before submission | **CONFIRMED** — minor cognitive gap | No major surprises. The component is more solid than I expected; the issues are concentrated in the announcement strategy. --- ## Critical Findings None. No finding blocks access entirely for any user category. All error information is reachable by all user groups. --- ## Major Findings ### 1. Dual error announcement: `role="alert"` + `aria-live="polite"` produce redundant screen reader output **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`, error summary block (lines with `role="alert"`) and inline error wrappers (lines with `aria-live="polite"`). When the form is submitted with 4 errors, the following sequence occurs: 1. **Assertive (interrupts):** `role="alert"` fires → *"There are 4 errors in this form. Email address is required. Password is required. Please confirm your password. Display name is required."* 2. **Polite (queued after):** All four `aria-live="polite"` regions update simultaneously → *"Email address is required." "Password is required." "Please confirm your password." "Display name is required."* The screen reader user hears **8 error messages** instead of 4. The polite announcements queue behind the assertive one, producing a confusing, redundant experience. **Why this matters:** This is the "Broadcast vs. Association" anti-pattern. The `role="alert"` on the summary already announces all errors. The `aria-live="polite"` wrappers add a second, redundant broadcast. The GOV.UK Design System pattern — which the developer's rationale explicitly cites — uses `role="alert"` on the summary and `aria-describedby` on fields, but does **not** add `aria-live` to inline errors. The `aria-describedby` association is sufficient: when the user navigates to a field, the screen reader reads the error via the description. No live region is needed for the initial announcement because the alert already covers it. **WCAG / APG citation:** WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages) — announcements should be specific and not redundant. WAI-ARIA APG "Form Validation" pattern — error messages are associated via `aria-describedby`, not broadcast via live regions when a summary already announces them. **User group impacted:** Screen reader users (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver). **Fix:** ```jsx // REMOVE aria-live from the inline error wrapper. // Keep the wrapper div for layout (min-height), but it should not be a live region.
{errors[name] && ( {errors[name]} )}
``` The `aria-describedby` on the input already associates the error. The `role="alert"` on the summary already announces all errors on submit. When the user navigates to a field, the screen reader reads the error via `aria-describedby`. When the user fixes a field, the error disappears — no announcement needed (the user knows they fixed it). **Confidence:** HIGH. The code unambiguously has both `role="alert"` and `aria-live="polite"` in the same render cycle. The GOV.UK pattern does not include both. --- ### 2. Error summary re-announces on every content change (user fixes one field → full summary re-read) **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`, error summary block. The summary is conditionally rendered (`{hasErrors && …}`) but remains in the DOM as long as *any* error exists. Its content changes when the user fixes one field (4 errors → 3 errors). Because `role="alert"` implies `aria-live="assertive"` + `aria-atomic="true"`, **every content mutation re-announces the full summary**. When the user fixes the email field: - The summary content changes from 4 `
  • ` items to 3 - The assertive live region fires → *"There are 3 errors in this form. Password is required. Please confirm your password. Display name is required."* - The user just fixed one field and is now hearing the remaining errors re-read in full This is a direct consequence of Finding #1's architecture. With the `aria-live="polite"` wrappers removed (per Finding #1's fix), the re-announcement is the *only* announcement, which is actually **useful** — it tells the user the error count changed. However, the assertive level is aggressive for an update that the user initiated. **Why this matters:** A screen reader user who fixes one of four errors and immediately hears the remaining three re-read in full (assertively, interrupting any in-progress speech) experiences a jarring, redundant interaction. The user already knows they fixed one field; they don't need the full summary re-read. **WCAG / APG citation:** WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages) — "Status messages should be announced with a level of urgency appropriate to the context." An update the user initiated does not require assertive urgency. **User group impacted:** Screen reader users. **Fix (recommended):** Change the error summary from `role="alert"` to `role="region"` with `aria-live="assertive"` and `aria-atomic="true"` for the initial appearance, but this doesn't solve the re-announcement. The better approach: **Option A (simplest, GOV.UK-aligned):** Keep `role="alert"`. Accept the re-announcement as a feature — it confirms the error count changed. The key fix is removing the `aria-live` from inline errors (Finding #1), which eliminates the *dual* announcement. The single re-announcement from the summary is tolerable. **Option B (more refined):** Use `role="alert"` for the initial appearance, then switch to `aria-live="polite"` after the first announcement. This requires a state flag: ```jsx const [summaryAnnounced, setSummaryAnnounced] = useState(false); // In the summary div:
    {/* ... */}
    // After initial focus + a short delay, flip the flag: useEffect(() => { if (hasErrors && !summaryAnnounced) { const t = setTimeout(() => setSummaryAnnounced(true), 1500); return () => clearTimeout(t); } }, [hasErrors, summaryAnnounced]); ``` This is more complex. **I recommend Option A** — keep `role="alert"`, remove the inline `aria-live`, and accept the re-announcement as a confirmation signal. It's simpler, matches GOV.UK, and the re-announcement is informative rather than harmful once the dual broadcast is eliminated. **Confidence:** HIGH. The re-announcement behavior of `role="alert"` on content change is well-documented across NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver. --- ## Minor Findings ### 3. Missing `autocomplete` attributes on all form fields **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`, the `fieldDefs` array and `` rendering. No `autocomplete` attribute is set on any input. Per WCAG 1.3.5 (Identify Input Purpose), form fields for personal data should use `autocomplete` to enable password managers, autofill, and assistive technology to identify the field's purpose. **Fix:** ```jsx const fieldDefs = [ { name: 'email', label: 'Email address', type: 'email', autocomplete: 'email' }, { name: 'password', label: 'Password', type: 'password', autocomplete: 'new-password' }, { name: 'confirmPassword', label: 'Confirm password', type: 'password', autocomplete: 'new-password' }, { name: 'displayName', label: 'Display name', type: 'text', autocomplete: 'name' }, ]; // In the input: ``` **User group impacted:** All users (password managers, autofill), especially cognitive accessibility users and users with motor impairments who benefit from autofill. **Confidence:** HIGH. The attributes are absent from the code. --- ### 4. No required-field indication before submission **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`. No `required` attribute, no `aria-required="true"`, no visual indicator (asterisk, "(required)" text) on any field. The only signal that a field is required is the error message after submission. A user filling out the form for the first time has no way to know which fields are mandatory until they submit and receive errors. This increases cognitive load and the likelihood of a failed first submission. **WCAG citation:** 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) — the relationship between the field and its required-ness should be programmatically exposed. **Fix:** ```jsx // Add to fieldDefs: { name: 'email', label: 'Email address', type: 'email', required: true, autocomplete: 'email' }, // ... // In the label: // In the input: ``` Add CSS for the asterisk: ```css .required-asterisk { color: #dc2626; } ``` **User group impacted:** Cognitive accessibility users, first-time users. **Confidence:** MEDIUM. The parent component or design system might handle required-ness indication externally, but it's absent from this component. --- ## Enhancements ### 5. Inline error text at 13px is below comfortable reading size **Evidence:** CSS `.error-text { font-size: 13px; }`. 13px is functional but small, especially for error messages that users need to read carefully. At 100% zoom, this is below the 16px minimum that most design systems recommend for body text. At 200% zoom (low vision users), it scales to 26px, which is fine. **Suggestion:** Increase to 14px minimum. Not a WCAG violation (WCAG has no minimum font size), but a best-practice improvement for readability. ### 6. Consider `aria-errormessage` for future-proofing **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`, `aria-describedby` usage. ARIA 1.2 introduced `aria-errormessage` as a more semantically precise attribute for error association. Browser support is now broad (Chrome 120+, Firefox 112+, Safari 17+). While `aria-describedby` is the correct choice today for maximum compatibility, noting `aria-errormessage` in a code comment or design system doc helps the team plan the migration: ```jsx // aria-describedby is used for maximum browser compatibility. // When ARIA 1.2 support is universal, migrate to aria-errormessage. aria-describedby={errors[name] ? `error-${name}` : undefined} ``` ### 7. Error summary links: consider programmatic focus for SPA robustness **Evidence:** `RegistrationForm.jsx`, ``. Hash links work in traditional browsers (the browser scrolls to the target and moves focus to the focusable element). However, in a React SPA with a client-side router, hash changes may be intercepted, causing a route change or no-op. A more robust pattern: ```jsx ``` This is a minor robustness improvement, not a WCAG violation. The current `` approach works in most contexts. --- ## What's Missing - **Success feedback:** After a valid submission (no errors), the form sets `submitted: true` and clears errors, but there is no success message, confirmation, or announcement. If the form stays on the page (no redirect), the user receives no feedback that their registration succeeded. If a parent component handles the redirect, this is fine — but it's not visible in this component. *(Open question — see below.)* - **Loading state:** If the form makes an API call on submit, there is no `aria-busy`, `role="status"`, or loading indicator. The submit button does not change to a "Submitting…" state. *(Open question — may be handled externally.)* - **`lang` attribute:** Not visible in this component (it's on ``). Not a finding for this component. - **Skip link:** Not applicable — this is a component, not a full page. --- ## Multi-Perspective Notes | Perspective | Alarm Level | Assessment | |-------------|-------------|------------| | **Screen reader** | **HIGH** | Dual announcement (Finding #1) and re-announcement (Finding #2) create a confusing, redundant experience. Semantic structure, labels, and `aria-describedby` are correct. The error summary links work for navigation. The primary issue is the announcement strategy, not the structure. | | **Keyboard-only** | **LOW** | Tab order is logical (summary → fields → submit). Error summary is focusable and receives focus on error. All interactive elements are keyboard-accessible. No traps. Focus indicators are visible. This perspective is well-served. | | **Low vision** | **LOW** | Color contrast meets 4.5:1 for all text. Focus indicators are visible (border color change + box-shadow on inputs, outline on summary and button). Touch targets meet 24×24 minimum. Error text at 13px is small but functional at 200% zoom. Links have underlines. No issues that would block low vision users. | | **Cognitive** | **MEDIUM** | Error messages are specific and actionable. Error summary provides a clear count and links. However, no required-field indication before submission (Finding #4) means the user must submit to discover which fields are mandatory. The dual announcement (Finding #1) adds cognitive load for screen reader users who must process redundant information. | | **Vestibular & motion** | **LOW** | No animations, transitions, or auto-playing content. N/A. | | **Auditory access** | **LOW** | No media elements. N/A. | | **Environmental contrast** | **LOW** | All contrast ratios meet WCAG 1.4.3. Color is not the sole indicator of error state (text + border + `aria-invalid`). No issues. | --- ## Verdict Justification **REVISE** — one targeted fix is required before shipping. The component's semantic structure, label associations, focus management, and keyboard operability are all sound. The developer correctly implemented the GOV.UK error summary pattern with `role="alert"`, `tabIndex={-1}`, programmatic focus, and `aria-describedby` associations. The heading hierarchy, form structure, and CSS focus indicators are correct. The single design flaw is the addition of `aria-live="polite"` to the inline error wrappers, which creates a dual announcement that the GOV.UK pattern does not include and that degrades the screen reader experience. The fix is to remove `aria-live="polite"` from the inline error wrapper divs (one attribute, four instances). Everything else — the `aria-describedby` associations, the `role="alert"` summary, the focus management, the semantic structure — is correct and should be preserved. **What would change this to ACCEPT:** Remove `aria-live="polite"` from the four inline error wrapper divs. Add `autocomplete` attributes. Optionally add required-field indication. **What would change this to REJECT:** Nothing. The component is functional and accessible. The issues are design refinements, not access blocks. --- ## Open Questions (unscored) 1. **Success feedback:** After a valid submission, does a parent component handle the redirect or show a success message? If the form stays on the page with no feedback, this is a MAJOR gap (no confirmation for any user). If a parent handles it, this is N/A. 2. **Loading state:** Does the form make an API call on submit? If so, is there a loading indicator (`aria-busy`, disabled submit button, `role="status"` message)? If not, the user has no feedback between clicking "Create account" and the response. 3. **SPA router interaction:** The error summary links use `href="#field-…"`. Does the application's router intercept hash changes? If so, the links may not scroll/focus as expected. Verify in the target environment. 4. **Design system context:** Is this component part of a design system that provides `autocomplete`, required-field indicators, and success feedback at a higher level? If so, Findings #3 and #4 may be handled externally. --- ## Self-Audit Summary | Finding | Confidence | Refutable? | Gap or Preference? | |---------|-----------|------------|--------------------| | #1 Dual announcement | HIGH | No — code unambiguously has both patterns | GAP | | #2 Re-announcement | HIGH | No — `role="alert"` behavior is well-documented | GAP (consequence of #1) | | #3 Missing autocomplete | HIGH | Possibly — parent component may add it | GAP | | #4 No required indication | MEDIUM | Possibly — design system may handle it | GAP | | #5 Font size 13px | HIGH | No — CSS is explicit | PREFERENCE (downgraded to Enhancement) | | #6 aria-errormessage | HIGH | No — not present | PREFERENCE (Enhancement) | | #7 SPA link robustness | MEDIUM | Yes — works in most browsers | PREFERENCE (Enhancement) | No findings were moved to Open Questions based on confidence. Findings #3 and #4 are noted as potentially handled externally.
